q: 1. 'Talus' is the soil transported by
explain: Talus (scree) is loose rock/soil debris that accumulates at the base of steep slopes or cliffs purely under the action of gravity, without any transporting medium like water, wind or ice.

q: 2. 'Loess' is silty clay formed by the action of
explain: Loess is a uniform, fine-grained (silt-sized) deposit laid down by wind (aeolian action) over long periods.

q: 3. 'Drift' is the material picked up, mixed, disintegrated, transported and re-deposited by
explain: Drift refers to all material transported and deposited by glaciers, either directly by moving ice or by the meltwater (glacier water) flowing from it.

q: 4. Non-cohesive soil is
explain: Sand consists of coarse, bulky grains with negligible inter-particle attraction, so it has no cohesion, unlike clay/silt which show cohesive behaviour.

q: 5. The soil transported by flowing water is called
explain: Soil carried and deposited by rivers/streams (flowing water) is termed alluvial soil.

q: 6. The soil transported by wind is called
explain: 'Aeolian' directly refers to wind-transported deposits such as loess and sand dunes.

q: 7. Lacustrine soils are those which are
options: deposited at the bottom of lakes
deposited due to moving of ice sheets
explain: 'Lacustrine' derives from Latin 'lacus' (lake); these soils settle out of still water at lake bottoms.

q: 8. Clay can be classified as
explain: Clay particles are extremely fine (<0.002 mm) with strong electro-chemical inter-particle attraction, making clay a highly cohesive soil.

q: 9. The degree of saturation in soils can be defined as the ratio of
options: water by weight to the dry soil weight
vol. of water to the gross vol. of soil
vol. of water to vol. of voids in soils
wt. of the water to wt. of soil
explain: Degree of saturation Sr = Volume of water / Volume of voids, expressed as a percentage; it tells how much of the void space is filled with water.

q: 10. The specific gravity of sand is approximately
explain: Sand is composed mainly of quartz, whose specific gravity is close to 2.65, commonly rounded to about 2.6.

q: 11. The most accurate method of determining the water content in a sample of soil is
explain: Oven drying at 105-110°C to constant weight removes only free/pore water precisely, making it the standard, most accurate laboratory method (IS: 2720 Part 2).

q: 12. Permeability of soil varies
options: inversely as square of grain size
explain: From Hazen's/Kozeny-type relations (k = C·D10²), coefficient of permeability is proportional to the square of the effective grain size.

q: 13. The coefficient of permeability is proportional to void ratio (e) as K = 100 D10² i.e., K ∝ D10²
explain: The Kozeny-Carman equation shows permeability is proportional to the function e³/(1+e), which accounts for void ratio's effect on flow paths.

q: 14. Maximum size of clay particle is
explain: By the standard grain-size classification, particles finer than 0.002 mm (2 microns) are classed as clay.

q: 15. Cohesionless soil is
explain: Sand grains are coarse and bulky with no significant surface attraction forces, so sand behaves as a cohesionless (frictional) soil.

q: 16. The height of capillary rise is maximum in
explain: Capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore/particle size; colloidal (extremely fine) soils have the smallest pores and hence the greatest capillary rise (though very slow).

q: 17. The soil which contains finest grain particles, is
explain: Clay has the smallest particle size (<0.002 mm) among the options, making it the finest-grained soil.

q: 18. The water content of soil is defined as the ratio of
options: volume of water to volume of given soil
volume of water to weight of air in voids
Weight of water to weight of air in voids
weight of water to weight of solids of given mass of soil
explain: Water content w = Weight of water / Weight of solids (dry weight), expressed as a percentage — the standard geotechnical definition.

q: 19. The relationship between void ratio (e) and porosity ratio (n) is:
explain: Since n = e/(1+e), rearranging gives e = n(1+e), the correct relation linking porosity and void ratio.

q: 20. A fundamental equation of void ratio (e), specific gravity (G), water content (ω) and degree of saturation (Sr) is
explain: From Se = wG (since Sr·e = w·G), rearranging gives e = wG/Sr, the fundamental phase-relationship equation.

q: 21. You are given a sample of soil containing coarse grains to determine its water content, you will use
explain: For coarse-grained soils, the pycnometer method (using known specific gravity) is the standard quick technique to back-calculate water content.

q: 22. The minimum water content at which the soil retains its liquid state and also possesses a small shearing strength against flowing, is known
explain: The liquid limit is the water content at the boundary between liquid and plastic states, where the soil just begins to show small shear resistance.

q: 23. The property of a soil which allows it to be deformed rapidly without rupture, elastic rebound and also a volume change, is known
explain: Plasticity is the property allowing rapid deformation without cracking, remoulding, and volume change, characteristic of fine-grained cohesive soils.

q: 24. For general engineering purposes, soils are classified by
explain: The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) is the most widely adopted system for general civil/geotechnical engineering purposes worldwide.

q: 25. Soils containing organic matters
options: shrink with increase of moisture content
explain: Organic soils (peats etc.) have a fibrous, porous, spongy texture due to decomposed plant matter, giving low bearing capacity and high compressibility.

q: 26. The change of moisture content of soils, changes the
options: value of the angle of repose
explain: Moisture content influences frictional/angle-of-repose behaviour, compaction effort needed, and cohesive strength — hence all listed properties are affected.

q: 27. The soil moisture driven off by heat, is called
explain: Hygroscopic (adsorbed) water is held tightly around particles by molecular attraction and is removed only by heating (oven drying), unlike free/gravity water.

q: 28. If a soil undergoes a change in shape and volume by application of external loads over it, but recovers its shape and volume immediately after removal of the load, the property of the soil to be
explain: Immediate and complete recovery of shape/volume after unloading is the defining characteristic of elastic behaviour.

q: 29. The capillary rise of water
options: increases as the size of the soil particles increases
decreases as the size of the soil particles decreases
is less in wet soil than in dry soil
explain: Capillary rise is governed by surface tension forces (menisci) at the air-water interface within the pores; hence it fundamentally depends on the responsible surface-tension force, and inversely on pore size.

q: 30. If the specific gravity and voids in soil sample are G and e respectively, the hydraulic gradient i, is
explain: The critical hydraulic gradient (at which quicksand condition occurs) is derived as icr = (G-1)/(1+e), balancing submerged weight against seepage force.

q: 31. Darcy's law is applicable to seepage if a soil is
explain: Darcy's law assumptions include a homogeneous, isotropic, saturated, incompressible medium with laminar flow — all conditions must hold.

q: 32. During seepage through a soil, direction of seepage is always
explain: In a flow net, flow lines (direction of seepage) always cross equipotential lines at right angles, i.e., seepage is perpendicular to equipotential lines.

q: 33. The quantity of seepage of water through soils is proportional to
options: total head loss through the soil
explain: By Darcy's law, q = k·i·A, and since i = head loss/length, seepage quantity is proportional to both permeability and total head loss.

q: 34. The phreatic line in an earth dam may be
explain: The top flow line (phreatic line) of seepage through an earth dam closely approximates a parabola (Casagrande's basic parabola method).

q: 35. The shear strength in plastic untrained clay, is due to
explain: In saturated plastic (undrained) clay tested quickly, pore pressures prevent frictional resistance from developing, so shear strength is essentially due to cohesion alone (φ=0 condition).

q: 36. The ultimate settlement of a soil is directly proportional to
options: depth of the compressible soil strata
explain: Consolidation settlement Sc = (Cc·H)/(1+e0)·log(...), directly proportional to both the thickness of compressible strata (H) and the compression index (Cc).

q: 37. The neutral stress in a soil mass is
options: stress taken up by the pore water
stress taken up by solid particles
explain: Neutral (pore-water) stress is the portion of total stress carried by water in the pores, as distinguished from effective stress carried by the soil skeleton.

q: 38. The shear strength of soil
options: increases with an increase in the normal stress
is proportional to the cohesion of the soil
is generally known as the strength of the soil
explain: By Coulomb's equation s = c + σ tanφ, shear strength increases with normal stress and cohesion, and is generally regarded as the overall 'strength' of soil — all statements are correct.

q: 39. For testing a saturated clay for shear strength, the test recommended, is
explain: For saturated clays, the quick, simple unconfined compression test is commonly recommended since no confining pressure is needed to get the undrained shear strength.

q: 40. On wetting, cohesive solid,
explain: Increased moisture reduces inter-particle attraction and increases pore pressure in cohesive soils, thereby decreasing their shear strength.

q: 41. The angle of internal friction of clays, is usually
explain: Because of their platy, fine particles and high cohesion, clays typically show a low drained friction angle in the range of about 5° to 20°.

q: 42. The angle of internal friction is maximum for
explain: Angular grains interlock more, and dense packing increases interlocking further, so angular-grained dense sand gives the highest angle of internal friction.

q: 43. The compression resulting from a long term static load and consequent escape of
explain: Consolidation is precisely the time-dependent compression caused by sustained static load driving pore water out of a saturated fine-grained soil.

q: 44. The reduction in volume of soil due to squeezing out of water from the voids, is termed
explain: The book lists all three terms (primary consolidation, primary compression, primary time effect) as synonymous descriptions of this volume-reduction phenomenon.

q: 45. The ratio of settlement at any time 't' to the final settlement, is known as
explain: Degree of consolidation U = settlement at time t / ultimate (final) settlement, a dimensionless fraction describing consolidation progress.

q: 46. The maximum pressure which a soil can carry without shear failure, is called
explain: Safe bearing capacity is the maximum pressure the soil can safely carry without shear failure, incorporating a factor of safety.

q: 47. The maximum net pressure intensity causing shear failure of soil, is known
explain: Net ultimate bearing capacity is defined as the net additional pressure (beyond overburden) that just causes shear failure of the foundation soil.

q: 48. The water content in a soil sample when it continues to loose weight without loosing the volume, is called
explain: Shrinkage limit is the water content below which further loss of moisture does not cause any further reduction in volume — i.e., weight reduces but volume stays constant.

q: 49. The density of soil can be increased
options: by reducing the space occupied by air
by elastic compression of soil grains
explain: Densification (compaction) can occur through expulsion of air, compression of grains, and expulsion of water — all mechanisms contribute to increasing density.

q: 50. When a cohesionless soil attains quick condition, it looses
explain: In quicksand condition, effective stress becomes zero due to upward seepage force equalling submerged weight, so the soil loses both its shear strength and bearing capacity.

q: 51. The coefficient of curvature is defined as
explain: Coefficient of curvature Cc = (D30)² / (D60 × D10), used along with Cu to assess gradation of a soil.

q: 52. The shearing strength of a cohesion less soil depends upon
explain: For cohesionless (frictional) soils, shear strength s = σ tanφ depends primarily on the normal/confining pressure acting on the failure plane.

q: 53. The soil transported by glaciers either by ice or water is called
explain: 'Drift' is the general term for material moved by glaciers, whether directly by ice movement or by glacial meltwater.

q: 54. Residual soils are
explain: Residual soils form in place by weathering of parent rock and can occur as sand, silt or clay depending on rock type and weathering degree — hence all of these.

q: 55. The property of a soil which is of great importance in finding settlement of structures, is
explain: Consolidation behaviour (rate and magnitude of volume change under load) directly governs long-term settlement calculations for structures.

q: 56. The ratio of the volume of voids to the total volume of soil mass is called
explain: Porosity n = Volume of voids / Total volume of soil mass, by definition.

q: 57. The ratio of the unit weight of soil solids to that of water is called
explain: Specific gravity G = unit weight (or density) of soil solids / unit weight (density) of water — the standard definition.

q: 58. Gravel and sand is a
explain: Gravel and sand are coarse-grained (particle size well above 0.075 mm) and lack cohesion, making them non-cohesive coarse-grained soils.

q: 59. The water content of soils can be accurately determined by
explain: Oven drying (105-110°C) is the standard, most accurate laboratory method for determining water content.

q: 60. The expression for the discharge (Q) through a flow net for isotropic soils is given by
explain: For an isotropic soil, seepage discharge Q = K·H·(Nf/Nd), where Nf is number of flow channels and Nd is number of potential drops.

q: 61. The degree of consolidation is proportional directly
options: to time and inversely to drainage path
to drainage path and inversely to time
to time and inversely to the square of drainage path
to square of drainage path and inversely to time
explain: The time factor Tv = Cv·t/d² shows degree of consolidation increases with time t and decreases with the square of the drainage path length d.

q: 62. Coarse grained soil contains material half of which is larger than
explain: As per soil classification (IS/USCS), a soil is termed coarse-grained if more than 50% of material by weight is retained on the 75-micron (0.075 mm) sieve.

q: 63. Liquid and plastic limit exists in the soil type
explain: Atterberg limits (liquid limit, plastic limit) are meaningful only for fine-grained, plastic soils such as clay, which exhibit plastic behaviour with changing moisture.

q: 64. Bearing capacity of soil depends up on the particle
explain: Bearing capacity is influenced by particle shape (interlocking), cohesion, and size (gradation/density) — collectively all these factors matter.

q: 65. Saturated clay test for shear strength can be performed by
explain: For saturated clay, the unconfined compression test directly gives the undrained shear strength without needing confining pressure, making it the simplest suitable test.

q: 66. The earth pressure in the retaining wall is
options: proportional to internal friction of the soil
explain: Lateral earth pressure at any depth p = K·γ·z increases linearly with depth z, so the pressure (intensity) itself is proportional to depth.

q: 67. One dimensional theory of Consolidation of Terzaghi is based on the assumption that
options: excess water is drained out only in the vertical direction
head is applied in one direction
explain: Terzaghi's 1-D consolidation theory assumes constant permeability, purely vertical drainage, and one-directional head/flow — all these assumptions together define the theory.

q: 68. On attaining quick condition, cohesionless soil loses its
explain: In quicksand condition, effective stress vanishes, so the soil loses both its bearing capacity and its shear strength simultaneously.

q: 69. Effective size of the particle is
explain: Effective size is defined as D10 — the particle size corresponding to 10% passing on the grain size distribution curve.
